To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
vaccination with plasmid‐encoding β cell autoantigan GAD could increase insulititis and diabetes in female NOD‐mice in correlation with a Th2/3 CD4 T cell response.
DNA vaccination encoding a major β cell autoantiegen can enhance insulits and diabetes in correlation to a specific Th2‐like CD4 T cell response.
DNA vaccination with GAD‐encoding plasmids enhanced diabetes incidence in correlation with a strong Th2‐like response in non‐ obese diabetic mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new aspect of DNA vaccination in autoimmune disease.
the potential risk of DNA vaccination against β cell autoantibodies.
the possibility that DNA‐vaccination may be used as a tool to study the pathogenesis of type I diabetes in NOD mouse model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GAD‐specific Th2/3 CD4 T cell response may have a dual role, either protective or destructive, depending on the context of the disease.
DNA vaccination against GAD may be deleterious for NOD mice.
GAD‐specific T cell immunity is a double‐edged sword in type I diabetes, depending on the cytokine profile of T cell responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DNA vaccination with a β cell autoantibody‐encoding plasmid may be deleterious in NOD mice.
DNA vaccination encoding GAD can enhance insulits and diabetes in correlation to a specific Th2 CD4 T cell response.
GAD‐based DNA vaccination can induce Th2/3‐type responses in NOD mice and this may be deleterious to β cell survival.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Th2/Th3 cells can be deleterious to β cells, in contrast to what was previously thought.
the Th2‐type response to GAD may be a risk factor for the onset and progression of type 1 diabetes.
DNA vaccination encoding GAD could be used to enhance insulitis in NOD mice, but that the resulting immune response should be carefully monitored.
